blocks.content: There shall be a High Court for each State.

rows: Wider (Article 226 - Fundamental Rights + Ordinary Legal Rights)

items: Parliament alone holds the authority to establish a common High Court for two or more states under Article 231, not the state legislatures.
The numerical strength of a High Court is decided flexibly by the President of India based on workload, unlike the Supreme Court where Parliament fixes judge strength.
Among Union Territories, Delhi and Jammu & Kashmir have dedicated High Courts, while others fall under the jurisdiction of neighboring State High Courts.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Article 214 of the Indian Constitution mandates that there shall be a High Court for each State.
The 7th Constitutional Amendment Act of 1956 empowered Parliament to establish a common High Court for two or more states or Union Territories.
The High Courts of Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras were the first to be established in India in 1862 under the Indian High Courts Act, 1861.
At present, India has 25 High Courts, with the Andhra Pradesh High Court at Amaravati being the 25th established in 2019.
The High Court occupies the top position in the judicial administration of a state, functioning below the Supreme Court.
